notes:
User is a Bay Area cyclist planning a roughly 10-day road trip next month, driving from San Francisco to New York City, with 3–4 days available for cycling. They want scenic, low-traffic routes and bike-friendly stops/shops and are comfortable with long rides and hills. Exact travel dates, start/end lodging, intended driving corridor, and which days will be cycling are not yet established. A prior proposed itinerary went via Lake Tahoe, Jackson Hole, Mount Rushmore, Minneapolis, and Pittsburgh, but its route times, trail claims, shops, and bike-storage properties were not verified and should be checked before relying on them.

They now have four bikes: a road bike, mountain bike, commuter bike, and a newly purchased hybrid. They are comfortable with the complexity of traveling with all four and plan to confirm in advance that lodging can securely store them. Vehicle capacity, bike rack/tracker, packing method, and whether all four bikes are truly needed remain unresolved. Advice to confirm bike storage, use secure racks/locks and covers, perform maintenance, and carry tools, tubes, and pump was welcomed.

They are especially interested in a guided mountain-bike tour around Jackson Hole for more challenging trails, while also considering local rentals and shops. Prior recommendations of specific operators, including those around Lake Tahoe, Jackson Hole, Mount Rushmore, Minneapolis, and Pittsburgh, may be inaccurate or stale and require verification of current operation, season, trail access, bike type, reservations, and guide availability.

The road bike has about 2,000 miles and is planned for long riding. They acquired a new bike computer and already track rides on Strava. Before the trip they should inspect/replace as needed: tires/tire age and pressure, chain, cassette, brake pads, cables/housing, and bearings; verify bolts; check frame/fork, saddle, bars, and electronic/accessory mounting; and ideally obtain a professional tune-up. Pack a compact repair kit and perform pre-ride checks. Fit, weather, route, nutrition, hydration, pacing, and support remain important. They previously considered carbon wheels, but the decision should be based on condition, budget, comfort, durability, crash/pothole exposure, brake compatibility, and whether basics or fit offer more value; 2,000 miles alone does not justify replacing them.

They recently bought new clipless cycling shoes and pedals and are adapting to clipless pedaling, which they feel has improved pedaling efficiency. They are considering whether to transport clipless pedals or keep platform pedals on the hybrid. Key guidance: only switch if the hybrid pedal threads/frame and cleats are compatible, the intended hybrid terrain is appropriate, and they are comfortable riding in clipless shoes; otherwise platforms are simpler and safer. If carrying road clipless pedals, they can be lightweight, but confirm drivetrain/pedal-thread compatibility and bring spare cleats. Since the road bike itself will already have pedals unless removed, confirm whether separate pedals are actually needed.

Other established interests include earlier Bay Area century planning and route ideas (Golden Gate–Sausalito/Marin Headlands, Mount Tam, Berkeley Hills, Dumbarton, Half Moon Bay/Pescadero/Santa Cruz), rear-derailleur adjustment topics, and researching a dedicated bike computer/Garmin Edge/Wahoo Elemnt/Lezyne products. Exact upcoming century route and start remain unknown.
trajectory:
User is a cyclist in the San Francisco Bay Area planning a 100-mile century ride soon. They have three bikes: a road bike used for weekend long rides and the planned century, a mountain bike used for trail rides, and a commuter bike used for daily commuting. They are comfortable owning three purpose-specific bikes and see the collection as useful rather than excessive.

The road bike has approximately 2,000 miles on it. They asked whether it is ready for a century and have been advised to inspect/replace worn tires, chain, cassette, brake pads, cables/housing, and bearings; verify all bolts; check frame/fork, saddle, and handlebars; and ideally get a professional tune-up. Fit, training, hydration, nutrition, pacing, and possibly group/support plans are also important. Existing long weekend rides are useful preparation, but prior mileage alone does not confirm readiness.

The user is considering upgrading the road bike’s wheels to carbon-fiber wheels. Their current wheels also have about 2,000 miles. They plan to research options further and consider budget before deciding. Relevant considerations: current wheel condition and safety, performance goals, comfort, weight, aerodynamics, durability, crash/pothole risk, brake and rim compatibility, total upgrade cost, and whether spending on wheels is better than tires, fit, drivetrain, brakes, or other needs. A professional mechanic/bike fitter’s input may be useful. Do not assume carbon wheels are needed merely because of the 2,000-mile usage.

Earlier topics included basic rear derailleur adjustment (limit screws, cable tension/barrel adjuster, hanger alignment and derailleur position, chain length, and incremental shifting tests) and Bay Area ride ideas such as the Golden Gate–Sausalito/Marin Headlands route, Mount Tamalpais, Berkeley Hills, Dumbarton Bridge area, and coastal routes toward Half Moon Bay/Pescadero/Santa Cruz. Exact century route and starting location have not been provided.

Latest request: recommendations for a dedicated bike computer/GPS instead of relying on phone GPS. Suggested brands/options so far include Garmin Edge, Wahoo Elemnt, and Lezyne. The eventual recommendation should be tailored to budget, navigation reliability, battery life, phone/ecosystem preference, mapping and turn-by-turn navigation, Strava/TrainingPeaks integration, sensors/antenna support (heart rate, cadence, power/temp), display/readability, phone-free operation, weather resistance, size/mounting, and total cost. Avoid implying every model includes heart-rate sensors; these often require separate accessories. Current market details and specific models should be verified before recommending.
